newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bomb defendants not expected at hearing.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bomb defendants not expected at hearing.

text.p: The defendants in the Oklahoma City bombing case will not appear at a pre-trial hearing next week when eyewitnesses who might be able to identify them are expected to be present, according to court filings Friday.
Timothy McVeigh and Terry Nichols, who are charged in the April 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building that claimed the lives of 168 people, have waived their right to be present.
Defence attorneys are expected to argue at the hearing Tuesday that the prosecution's eyewitnesses should not be allowed to testify against the defendants.
Prosecutors have said in court filings that eyewitnesses at several places in Kansas, where the alleged truck bomb purportedly was built, and Oklahoma can tie McVeigh and Nichols to the bombing.

But the defendants' attorneys claim that testimony by the eyewitnesses should be barred on grounds that it is unreliable. McVeigh's attorneys claim, for example, that the eyewitnesses are confused because they saw the defendants' pictures many times in news photographs.
The two defendants will be tried separately, with McVeigh going first, on March 31. Nichols will be tried at a later undetermined date.
At a separate hearing Wednesday, defence attorneys will renew their attack on prosecutors' plans to use handwriting and hair samples from the defendants as evidence against them.
Friday, U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch ruled that testimony from a key prosecution witness will be allowed in the trial over defence objections.

Defence lawyers had objected to the testimony of Thomas Manning, manager of a tire story where McVeigh bought a car four days before the bombing and which he was driving when arrested, because Manning remembered 18 months later that McVeigh left the store for several minutes.
Prosecutors contend that during that interval McVeigh telephoned Nichols and also the rental truck agency where he allegedly rented the Ryder truck purportedly used in the bombing.
Defence attorneys suggested that Manning's new information may have been the result of prompting by prosecutors, but the judge said there was no evidence to support that claim.
